newsitem.title: GERMANY: German SPD denies plans to work with communists.
newsitem.headline: German SPD denies plans to work with communists.

text.p: Bonn's opposition Social Democrats (SPD) on Friday denied charges they planned to link up with reform communists in east Germany to outflank Chancellor Helmut Kohl after the next general election in 1998.

Party chairman Oskar Lafontaine ruled out any national coalition with the Party of Democratic Socialism (PDS), successors to the hardline communists who ruled East Germany with an iron fist until the Berlin Wall fell in 1989.

But he left open the option for "popular front" governments after polls in 1999 in the five east German states, a prospect that prompted seven eastern civil rights campaigners to leave the ecologist Greens and SPD parties this week to join the CDU.
Boosted by the defections, the CDU is already planning an aggressively anti-communist campaign to keep the divided SPD on the defensive like it did successfully in 1994.

CDU strategists were also heartened this week by a position paper by east German SPD leader Wolfgang Thierse that said the SPD probably had no alternative to cooperating in the east with the PDS, which has a firm 20 percent of the vote there.
Any SPD-PDS link would be anathema to most west German voters, who make up 80 percent of the electorate and care little about the different political situation in the east.
"The paper said there would be no cooperation between the SPD and the PDS to defeat the present national government," Lafontaine told Der Spiegel magazine.
Asked whether his party would accept such left-wing pacts on the state level, he said: "We're not going to cackle over eggs before they laid."

Seven years after Germany reunited in 1990, the political scene seems stuck at a near checkmate between Kohl's centre- right coalition and the combined opposition of SPD, Greens and PDS. Even after the defections, Kohl has only a tight 12-seat majority in a parliament with 672 members.

The PDS, now a self-styled socialist party defending east German interests, remains such a political pariah that the SPD agreed to be junior partners in CDU-led coalitions in three states -- Berlin, Mecklenburg-Vorpommern and Thuringia -- rather than opt for a controversial coalition with it.

Eastern SPD leaders have slowly been moving towards accepting some kind of link with the PDS. In Saxony-Anhalt state, a minority SPD-Greens coalition already governs with the tacit approval of the PDS.

Kohl and CDU general secretary Peter Hintze, who managed a skillful 1994 reelection campaign accusing the SPD of flirting with ex-Stalinists, have been trying to widen the CDU's base by wooing former eastern civil rights activists disillusioned with western left-wing parties.

This week' defections included only one Bonn deputy, the former Green Vera Lengsfeld, a one-time dissident whom the communists expelled to Britain in 1988 and whose husband informed on her for the hated Stasi security police.
But commentators say they may have broken the ice in east Germany and been the opening shot in a 1998 CDU campaign.

"The SPD and the Greens will have to be prepared for the Red Socks campaign," Munich's Sueddeutsche Zeitung said, referring to Hintze's 1994 anti-communist drive, "and for being led around by the nose on a ring marked PDS."
